title: Area IV review: Preflight Lesson on a Maneuver to be Performed in Flight
intro: One Task, twelve questions: the maneuver briefing an evaluator asks you to deliver. They mix purpose, elements and errors, completion standards, risk and teaching methods, using slow flight and ground reference maneuvers as the sample maneuvers.

questions.q: You are briefing slow flight to a 10-hour learner. After yesterday's flight your notes show deviations of altitude plus or minus 70 feet, heading plus or minus 8 degrees, airspeed plus 7 and minus 0 knots, and bank plus or minus 8 degrees. Which statement is accurate, and what do you tell the learner today?
options: The numbers are inside the private and commercial tolerances and miss only the CFI tolerance, so the learner is almost ready for the checkride standard
The numbers are inside the private tolerances on all four items but outside the commercial and CFI tolerances for altitude, airspeed and bank, so they fit this stage and set the next target
The airspeed is outside the private tolerance, because the private ACS allows only plus 5 and minus 0 knots
The numbers are inside all three tolerance sets, because the heading deviation of 8 degrees is within the plus or minus 10 degrees all three share
questions.why: Private slow flight standards are altitude plus or minus 100 feet, heading plus or minus 10 degrees, airspeed plus 10 and minus 0 knots, and bank plus or minus 10 degrees (ACS PA.VII.A.S5). All four of the learner's numbers fit. Commercial and CFI are altitude plus or minus 50 feet, airspeed plus 5 and minus 0 knots and bank plus or minus 5 degrees (ACS CA.VII.A.S5, AI.X.A.S5); 70 feet, plus 7 knots and 8 degrees all miss those, and only the heading fits. The +5/-0 knot limit is not the private one. Assessment uses standards suitably modified for the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and lesson standards grow toward the ACS over time [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

questions.q: You plan to brief a rectangular course at 1,000 feet AGL, the top of the usual 600 to 1,000 foot range. The map shows a 640-foot AGL radio tower about 1,500 feet from the nearest leg of your planned track. What do you brief?
options: Keep 1,000 feet AGL and tell the learner to watch the tower, since obstruction clearance applies only to the maneuver altitude and not to the distance from the track
It is fine, because 1,000 feet AGL is inside the 600 to 1,000 foot range the AFH gives for ground reference maneuvers
Drop to 600 feet AGL so the airplane passes well below the top of the tower
Neither clearance is met: 360 feet above the tower is short of 500, and 1,500 feet is short of 2,000 horizontally, so move the maneuver away from it
questions.why: The AFH says the altitude you pick should provide obstruction clearance of no less than 500 feet vertically above the obstruction and 2,000 feet horizontally [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Here 1,000 minus 640 is 360 feet, under 500 feet, and 1,500 feet is under 2,000 feet, so neither is met. The 600 to 1,000 foot range is a general guide and does not override the clearance. Dropping to 600 feet is worse: it would put the airplane lower than the tower top and cut engine-out time and glide distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Brief the tower as a hazard and move the maneuver to a better area.

questions.q: Just before your ground brief on slow flight and stalls, a 10-hour learner says: "I have to finish this stage today, my job interview is Friday and my schedule is full." He is rushing and tense. Which risk category is this, and what does the AIH tell you to do?
options: Pilot: treat it as an IMSAFE stress item and brief faster, so that the whole lesson still fits in the time he has before his Friday interview
Environment: nothing to do, because only weather and terrain count as hazards for a maneuver brief
External pressure: acknowledge the schedule, say changes are fine, and be ready to switch to classroom work or end early if he stays tense
Aircraft: nothing to do, because time pressure affects only the learner's own preparation
questions.why: PAVE has four buckets, and the AIH discusses external pressure as its own risk category [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Schedule and job demands are external pressures, which the AIH calls the most insidious hazards. Instructors should ease the concerns, stress that schedule changes are acceptable, and be ready to change from airplane to classroom instruction or end the lesson early if the learner seems apprehensive about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Briefing faster does not fix this: it is not a pilot-health item, and a rushed brief leaves the learner less prepared, which the AIH names as a serious hazard [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

questions.q: Planning a rectangular course brief, you pick a large rectangular field. A county fair crowd is gathered in the open next to it, and a herd of cattle grazes on the far side. Your planned 800 feet AGL clears every obstruction. What do you brief?
options: Keep the field: 800 feet AGL already gives the 500-foot vertical clearance the AFH asks for from obstructions
Keep the field, but fly at 1,000 feet AGL so the crowd and the cattle are not disturbed by the noise
Pick another area: the AFH says to stay well away from open-air assemblies of people and herds of livestock
Keep the field and fly the course only on the side away from the fair, since the cattle do not matter
questions.why: The maneuver area should not cause disturbances and should be well away from any open air assembly of persons, congested areas of a city, town or settlement, or herd of livestock. The pilot also clears the area with two 90° clearing turns and has one or more emergency landing locations [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Obstruction clearance alone does not settle the choice of area.

questions.q: The evaluator says, "Give me your slow flight preflight lesson," and says nothing about who the learner is. What do the sources point you to first?
options: Ask about the learner, since the objectives rest on the learner's known experience and knowledge
Teach it to the CFI ACS standard, since the evaluator is the one who will judge the lesson
Skip the objective and standards, since the evaluator already knows them from the ACS
Deliver the plan exactly as written, since a lesson plan is meant to be the same for every learner
questions.why: In the explanation phase the instructor presents objectives based on the known experience and knowledge of the learner [[25:175|AIH 9-5]], and a lesson plan should fit the learner's background, experience and ability; even a preprinted plan may need changes for a specific learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]]. The Area IV note in the CFI ACS asks for the lesson as it would be taught to a student, so ask who that student is.

questions.q: Your private pilot learner asks whether your CFI checkride holds the rectangular course to tighter numbers than her private checkride. What is accurate?
options: Yes: the CFI standard is altitude ±50 feet and airspeed ±5 knots, as for slow flight
Yes: the CFI standard adds a heading tolerance of ±10 degrees on each leg
No: the CFI ACS sets no numbers, since the instructor only teaches the maneuver
No: both hold altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots
questions.why: For the rectangular course, the private and CFI ACS both say maintain altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.V.B.S7, AI.IX.E.S7). The ±50 feet and +5/-0 knots belong to the commercial and CFI slow flight standards (ACS CA.VII.A.S5, AI.X.A.S5). Your lesson standards for her are set for her stage and grow toward the ACS [[25:182|AIH 9-12]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

questions.q: In your slow flight brief you say you will have the learner roll into a level turn at the slow flight speed. What do you tell the learner to expect and do to hold altitude in the turn?
options: Hold the same power and pull back more, since the elevator holds altitude
Add power during the turn to maintain altitude
Reduce power slightly so the angle of attack stays unchanged
Retract the flaps one notch at the start of the turn to reduce drag
questions.why: In slow flight turns it is necessary to increase power to maintain altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. At this speed any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor or reduction in power will result in a stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], so more back pressure or less power is the wrong direction. Abrupt flap retraction in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Brief the turn as its own element, because the learner who forgets the extra power sees an altitude loss and a stall warning.

questions.q: Your slow flight brief reaches its last element, the exit back to cruise. Which sequence do you brief?
options: Raise the flaps first to cut drag and let the airplane accelerate on its own, then add power once it is clean and trimmed again
Lower the nose first to build airspeed with the power left at the slow flight setting, then add power when the airspeed is back near cruise
Add power, then forward pressure to hold altitude as speed builds; stay coordinated, then retract flaps and gear and adjust trim, expecting the AOA change
Add full power and keep the back pressure where it is, so the airplane climbs away from the stall and the flaps come up in the climb
questions.why: To exit slow flight, add power; as airspeed and lift increase, apply forward control pressure to reduce the AOA and maintain altitude, and maintain coordinated flight. As airspeed increases, retract the flaps and gear and adjust trim, anticipating the AOA changes to avoid a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Abruptly raising the flaps in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], so they do not come first. Lowering the nose before adding power gives up altitude, and holding the back pressure with full power keeps the AOA high.

questions.q: You brief a rectangular course for a left pattern with the wind from the south. The learner enters on the east leg flying north. On your marker board you ask which turn needs the shallowest bank, rolled in slowly, and ends with less than 90 degrees of heading change. Which turn is it?
options: From the south-flying upwind leg onto the east-flying crosswind leg
From the west-flying base leg onto the south-flying upwind leg
From the east-flying crosswind leg onto the north-flying downwind leg
From the north-flying downwind leg onto the west-flying base leg
questions.why: Wind from the south makes the north-flying leg the downwind leg. Left turns take the airplane west on the base leg, south on the upwind leg, then east on the crosswind leg. The turn from upwind to crosswind starts at the lowest groundspeed, so it takes a shallow bank rolled in slowly while the crosswind drifts the airplane to the inside. The airplane then holds an angle into the wind toward the outside, so the turn is less than 90 degrees [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Downwind to base is steep and more than 90 degrees. Base to upwind is medium and less than 90 degrees. Crosswind to downwind is medium and more than 90 degrees [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. The higher the groundspeed, the steeper the bank [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

questions.q: You are briefing why bank must change around the rectangular course. Your airplane flies 100 knots true airspeed, and the wind is 20 knots straight down the downwind leg and straight up the upwind leg. Using radius = V squared / (g x tan bank), with V in feet per second and g = 32.174, you plan a 45 degree bank at the start of the downwind turn. About what bank holds the same ground radius when the groundspeed is lowest on the upwind side?
options: 24 degrees
34 degrees
About 30 degrees
18 degrees
questions.why: Downwind groundspeed is 120 knots, or 202.5 feet per second. The radius is 202.5 squared divided by (32.174 x tan 45), about 1,275 feet. Upwind groundspeed is 80 knots, or 135.0 feet per second, so tan bank = 135.0 squared / (32.174 x 1,275) = 0.444, and the bank is 24.0 degrees. The answer 30 comes from scaling the bank linearly (45 x 80/120), which overstates it, because tan bank changes with the square of groundspeed. The AFH shows the same pattern: 45 degrees at 100 knots groundspeed needs about 33 degrees at 80 knots [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. Higher groundspeed means steeper bank, lower means shallower [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

questions.q: A school is moving to scenario-based training (SBT). A colleague tells you the new plan format means you no longer need a stand-alone lesson to teach slow flight. What does the AIH say?
options: He is right only for private pilot training; commercial and CFI training must stay maneuver-based, so slow flight keeps its own lesson only there
He is right: SBT replaces maneuver training, so maneuvers are learned only inside scenarios
He is wrong: the SBT plan allows maneuvers but leaves out completion standards and hazards
He is wrong: maneuvers needing repetition are still taught in concentrated sessions, then built into realistic flights
questions.why: SBT does not preclude traditional maneuver-based training. Flight maneuvers are integrated into scenarios, and those needing repetition are still taught in concentrated settings, then integrated into realistic flight situations [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. The SBT plan adds a type of training, a scenario, possible hazards with a mitigating strategy, and a postflight review that usually begins with the learner's self-critique; it still carries completion standards [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Plan format should be adapted to the learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

questions.q: A 14-hour learner asks, "Why do we spend whole lessons on rectangular courses and turns around a point? I already fly the pattern." Which answer best delivers the purpose of the maneuver (K1) in the brief?
options: Because the private ACS requires ground reference maneuvers and you will be tested on them

Because these maneuvers combine the four fundamentals into integrated skills used from every takeoff to every landing, and the rectangular course replicates the traffic pattern, so it prepares you for pattern and landing practice
Because flying low over the ground is the best place to practice stall recovery
Because they are the only way to learn to fly a 45 degree bank, which you need in the pattern
questions.why: The AFH calls ground reference maneuvers the principal maneuvers that combine the four fundamentals into integrated skills used in everyday flight, from every takeoff to every landing [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. The rectangular course replicates the traffic pattern and prepares the pilot for the pattern and subsequent landing pattern practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. "It is on the checkride" is not a purpose; the ACS is a testing document and lessons should not focus on the minimum for passing [[24:30|AFH 1-9]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Banks should stay at 45 degrees or less [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], and stall practice is not the purpose.
